title: Why memory is slow in the first place
kicker: 11 · Why memory is slow in the first place

scenes.name: six transistors against one capacitor
scenes.visual: A physical circuit comparison between an SRAM cell and a DRAM cell. On the left, an SRAM cell built from six transistors forming two stable cross-coupled feedback loops. On the right, a DRAM cell consisting of a single transistor and a tiny microscopic capacitor that visibly leaks electrical charge over time.

beats.say: The memory hierarchy is not an arbitrary design choice. It follows directly from the physics of a memory cell.
beats.show: Two circuit diagrams appear side by side: left labeled 'SRAM cell (on-chip)', right labeled 'DRAM cell (off-chip)'.

beats.say: An S RAM cell uses six transistors to form two loops that actively reinforce each other. It can be read in a single cycle without disturbing its state.
beats.show: In the left panel, six transistors illuminate with active feedback loops. A read probe measures the voltage instantly with zero signal degradation.

beats.say: A D RAM cell uses just one transistor and one tiny capacitor. The bit is stored as a microscopic packet of electrical charge.
beats.show: In the right panel, a single transistor controls access to a tiny capacitor plate. A full charge represents '1'; an empty charge represents '0'.

beats.say: Because it uses one transistor instead of six, D RAM is far denser and cheaper per bit: that is how eighty gigabytes fits beside the chip. But a capacitor leaks like a bucket with a hole.
beats.show: Density visual: six DRAM cells fit in the footprint of one SRAM cell. An animated gauge shows the capacitor voltage slowly leaking downward toward zero. Takeaway: 'SRAM is fast but bulky; DRAM is dense but physically leaky'.

scenes.name: destructive read and the refresh timer
scenes.visual: A cycle diagram showing what happens during a DRAM read: measuring the charge drains the capacitor, forcing a mandatory rewrite cycle. A separate periodic timeline shows rows being refreshed every 64 milliseconds.

beats.say: Reading a D RAM cell destroys the bit. The stored charge is so small that measuring it drains it completely.
beats.show: A read operation connects to the capacitor. The electrical charge flows out into the sense amplifier, leaving the capacitor completely empty.

beats.say: Every read is therefore a read followed by an immediate rewrite, and that memory row is blocked until the rewrite finishes.
beats.show: A two-phase sequence executes: phase 1 'read & drain', phase 2 'rewrite & restore'. A lock icon seals the row during the rewrite.

beats.say: Because the charge leaks away continuously, the memory controller must also rewrite every row on a timer: every sixty-four milliseconds.
beats.show: A circular refresh timer sweeps: '64 millisecond refresh window'. Rows across the DRAM array pulse green as they are refreshed sixteen times every second.

beats.say: These physical constraints make D RAM slower to respond. But they do not limit bandwidth: bandwidth comes from wires.
beats.show: A summary card balances the trade: 'DRAM physics sets latency; wire count sets bandwidth'.

scenes.name: the two hundred and seventy nanosecond journey
scenes.visual: A timeline breakdown of one 273-nanosecond HBM load. The actual capacitor readout takes only 27.5 nanoseconds; the other 90% is physical signal transit, cache checks, crossbar arbitration, and memory controller queues.

beats.say: When a thread requests a number from high-bandwidth memory, the journey takes about two hundred and seventy-three nanoseconds.
beats.show: A full timeline bar draws to 273 nanoseconds, labeled 'One HBM memory load · ~273 ns (479 clock ticks)'.

beats.say: The memory cell itself takes only twenty-seven point five nanoseconds to open a row and read a column: barely a tenth of the total time.
beats.show: A small sliver at the far right highlights: 'cell activation & column read · 27.5 ns (10% of total)'.

beats.say: Most of the wait is the journey: checking local caches, crossing the chip to the memory controller, waiting in queues, and traveling across package traces.
beats.show: The remaining 90% of the timeline expands into transit stages: 'L1 check → crossbar transit → memory controller queue → PHY bus'.

beats.say: Wider buses do not shorten that journey. More wires carry more bytes at once, but they do not make signals travel faster across silicon.
beats.show: A bus widens from 1,000 wires to 5,000 wires. The volume increases, but the transit latency remains fixed at 273 nanoseconds. Takeaway: 'bandwidth scales with wires; latency is bounded by physical transit distance'.

scenes.name: why there must be a ladder
scenes.visual: A 2D scatter plot of storage technologies: Speed on the vertical axis versus Capacity on the horizontal axis. Registers sit at top-left; DRAM sits at bottom-right. The top-right corner is physically empty.

beats.say: In every computer ever built, storage technologies face the exact same trade: speed against capacity.
beats.show: An XY chart draws: vertical axis 'Speed (latency)', horizontal axis 'Capacity (bytes)'. Storage technologies plot as points.

beats.say: The top-right corner is completely empty. No technology exists that is both the fastest and the largest.
beats.show: A bright spotlight highlights the empty top-right corner: 'impossible: fast and vast'.

beats.say: Speed requires physical proximity: to be fast, a memory must be microscopic and sit right next to the arithmetic.
beats.show: A diagram shows registers wrapped tightly around the math units: 'fast requires physical closeness'.

beats.say: Large capacity requires surface area, which inevitably pushes memory further away across longer wires. The only possible solution is a ladder.
beats.show: A four-rung ladder draws upward connecting HBM to L2, L1, and registers. Takeaway pill: 'speed requires proximity, capacity requires area: memory must be a ladder'.

checks.claim: Cell read time: row open 13.75 ns + column read 13.75 ns = 27.5 ns, which is about one tenth of 273 ns (10.07%)
Refresh interval: 64 ms / 8,192 commands = 7.8125 microseconds per command
Full refresh rate: 1 / 64 ms = 15.625 full rewrites per second, quoted as 'sixteen times every second'
